content: 1. The effectiveness of various malaria interventions needs to be evaluated in different settings, as the vector species may vary. Detailed descriptions of the interventions, the types of larval habitats, and the targeted vector species are essential. This includes understanding the physical properties of the habitats being modified, such as water flow, volume, sunlight penetration, salinity, or other conditions. 2. The impact of using larvivorous fish on malaria incidence (both infection and clinical cases) and prevalence, as well as any potential harms or unintended consequences, must be determined. 3. Further evidence is required to assess the impact of topical repellents on malaria incidence and prevalence, as well as any potential harms or unintended consequences, particularly in high-risk populations such as migrants, refugees, forest-goers, military personnel, and those who sleep outdoors. 4. Additional evidence is needed to evaluate the impact of topical repellents on individuals who use them, including their effects on malaria incidence and prevalence, and any associated harms or unintended consequences. 5. The impact of topical repellents on populations living in African settings, including their effects on malaria incidence and prevalence, and any potential harms or unintended consequences, must be further studied. 6. Evidence is needed to assess the impact of topical repellents against Plasmodium vivax malaria, including their effects on malaria incidence and prevalence, and any potential harms or unintended consequences. 7. Factors such as acceptability, feasibility, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, and user preferences related to the use of topical repellents should be evaluated. 8. The impact of insecticide-treated clothing on malaria incidence and prevalence, as well as any potential harms or unintended consequences, should be determined in the general population. 9. Approaches to improve the acceptability and desirability of WHO guidelines for malaria prevention, as well as strategies to increase uptake and adherence, should be identified. 10. Insecticidal formulations that enhance the durability of efficacy should be developed. 11. The impact of spatial or airborne repellents on malaria incidence and prevalence, as well as any potential harms or unintended consequences, should be determined. 12. Long-lasting spatial repellent insecticide formulations should be developed. 13. Epidemiological and entomological evidence is needed to determine whether repellents cause the diversion of malaria mosquitoes from treated areas to neighboring untreated areas. 14. The impact of space spraying on malaria incidence and prevalence, as well as any potential harms or unintended consequences, particularly in emergency situations, should be evaluated. 15. Further evidence is required to assess the impact of house screening and other housing modifications, either alone or in combination, on malaria incidence and prevalence, as well as any potential harms or unintended consequences. 16. Epidemiological evidence is needed to evaluate the efficacy of the same intervention implemented in different settings where vector species may differ. 17. The resource needs, costs, and cost-effectiveness of various deployment options for house screening (at the program, community, and individual levels) should be determined. 18. Deployment mechanisms and strategies to foster community buy-in for house screening and other housing modifications should be developed. 19. The impact of different strategies for insecticide resistance management, such as insecticide rotations or mosaics, on malaria incidence and prevalence should be determined. 20. The impact of insecticide resistance on key outcomes, including malaria mortality, clinical disease, and infection prevalence, should be evaluated. 21. Potential harms or unintended consequences of vector control interventions, such as undesirable effects on individuals, communities, mosquito biology, and the environment, should be considered. 22. Structural challenges, opportunities, acceptability, feasibility, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, values, and preferences related to vector control interventions in stable and humanitarian emergency settings should be assessed. 23. Evidence on the use of tools to monitor recommended vector control interventions should be gathered. 24. Evidence supporting the prioritization of interventions, including their benefits and potential harms, should be provided to guide decision-making. 25. Preventive chemotherapies, such as chemoprevention and chemoprophylaxis, use antimalarial medicines to prevent malaria infection and disease. Chemoprevention involves full therapeutic courses of antimalarial medicines at prescheduled times to treat existing infections and prevent new ones, reducing malaria in endemic areas. 26. Chemoprophylaxis typically involves sub-therapeutic doses of antimalarials to prevent new infections and is primarily used by non-immune individuals traveling to malaria-endemic areas. 27. Current WHO recommendations for chemoprevention include intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp), perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC), seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), intermittent preventive treatment in school-aged children (IPTsc), post-discharge malaria chemoprevention (PDMC), mass drug administration (MDA), and mass relapse prevention. 28. IPTp involves administering antimalarial medicines at predetermined intervals during pregnancy, regardless of infection status, to reduce disease burden and adverse pregnancy outcomes. 29. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) is widely used for malaria chemoprevention during pregnancy and remains effective in improving key pregnancy outcomes. 30. IPTp-SP should start as early as possible in the second trimester, but not before week 13 of pregnancy, and doses should be given at least one month apart to ensure at least three doses are received. 31. Antenatal care (ANC) remains a critical platform for delivering IPTp, but alternative delivery methods, such as community health workers, may be explored to address inequities in ANC service delivery. 32. IPTp is highly cost-effective, widely accepted, feasible for delivery, and supported by extensive evidence. 33. In areas of moderate to high Plasmodium falciparum transmission, IPTp-SP should be given to all pregnant women. 34. The role of IPTp in areas with low malaria transmission levels remains uncertain, and there is insufficient data to define the transmission level below which IPTp-SP may no longer be cost-effective. 35. Discontinuing IPTp-SP following a recent reduction in malaria transmission should be approached with caution, as reintroduction may pose challenges. 36. IPTp improves a wide range of outcomes in women during their first and second pregnancies, including maternal and placental infection, maternal anemia, and low birth weight. 37. Administering IPTp to all pregnant women, regardless of the number of pregnancies, simplifies implementation for health workers. 38. IPTp-SP should ideally be administered as directly observed therapy (DOT) with three tablets of SP, providing a total dosage of 1500 mg/75 mg SP. 39. IPTp-SP should not be given before week 13 of pregnancy due to an increased risk of fetal malformation. It should start in the second trimester and be given at each scheduled ANC contact until delivery, provided doses are at least one month apart. 40. At least three doses of IPTp-SP should be received during pregnancy to ensure optimal protection.
